result:
The rain came sideways that Tuesday, needling the windows of the coffee shop on Mercer Street where I'd been sitting for the better part of three hours, nursing a cold latte and watching the world blur into a watercolor of umbrellas and headlights. The barista had stopped glancing at me around hour two, which was a small mercy. I had a laptop open in front of me, cursor blinking in an empty document, and I was supposed to be writing something brilliant about urban infrastructure or maybe the gentrification of Brooklyn neighborhoods. The piece was due Friday. I had not started it.

Instead, I was thinking about my grandmother, who had died two weeks earlier in a hospice in Phoenix under a sky so blue it looked painted. She was ninety-three and had outlived three husbands, two of her three children, and most of her teeth. Her name was Dolores, which she hated, and she made me call her Dot. The last coherent thing she said to me was, "Don't let the bastards get you down," which she had been saying to me since I was six years old, though she had never specified who the bastards were. I suspected, sometimes, that she meant everyone. She was a happy woman, all things considered, and I think that's the thing I will miss most—that particular lightness she carried, like a song she'd been humming her whole life and had simply never bothered to stop.

I should have been at the funeral. I wasn't. I was in New York, where I had been for eleven years, building a life that looked, from the outside, like exactly the kind of life a person is supposed to want. I had an apartment with a view of a brick wall. I had a job that paid me to write sentences nobody would read carefully. I had a plant named Gerald who was, I was fairly certain, dying. I had people I called friends, though I could count on one hand the number of them I would have called at three in the morning, and most of those calls would have been to apologize for not calling sooner. I had a recurring subscription to a meditation app I never opened. I had a mother who called every Sunday and asked, with increasing urgency, when I was going to come home, by which she meant Ohio, by which she meant her house, by which she meant the bedroom I had slept in until I was twenty-two and where, she hinted with the subtlety of a stage whisper, there would always be a place for me.

I was thirty-four. I had stopped making sense of my life somewhere around twenty-nine, and I had been treading water ever since, very stylishly, in a way that fooled almost everyone, including, on most days, myself.

Outside, the rain intensified. A woman came in shaking out her umbrella, a small tornado of a person with bright red hair and a coat the color of a stop sign. She ordered something complicated and waited at the pickup counter with the particular focus of someone who is trying not to look at anyone else. I recognized the posture. It is the posture of a person who has just lost something and is not yet ready to be perceived.

I looked away. I had lost something too, recently, and I was not yet ready to be perceived either, though I could not have told you what it was, exactly. I had not lost a person, not really—Dot was ninety-three, and she had been leaving for years, the way the tide goes out, slowly and then all at once. I had not lost a job or a lover or a home. What I had lost, I think, was the particular fiction I had been telling myself, which was that I had time. That I would, at some unspecified future point, get around to the things I kept meaning to get around to. That Dot would be there when I finally did. That the world would wait.

The world, of course, does not wait. The world has never waited for anyone. This is not a new observation, but it had the bite of a new one, and I sat with it for a while, the way you sit with a sore tooth, pressing on it gently just to feel the hurt.

I closed the laptop. The barista, a kid with a nose ring and a posture that suggested he had been told, recently and by someone authoritative, to stand up straight, caught my eye. "Refill?" he asked.

"No, thank you," I said. "I'm going to go."

"Got everything you need?"

I thought about this. I thought about it for longer than the question probably warranted, and he waited, which was kind of him, and I appreciated it in a way I could not have explained. "No," I said finally. "But I'm going to go anyway."

He nodded, as if this were a perfectly reasonable thing to say, and perhaps to him it was. I left too large a tip. I put on my coat. I stepped out into the rain, which had softened to a kind of mist, and walked north, without destination, without plan, the way a person walks when they have finally understood that the walking is the point, and the arriving is optional, and the bastards, whoever they are, are not going to get me down, not today, not if Dot had anything to say about it, and Dot, wherever she was now, probably had plenty to say about everything, and was probably saying it, loudly, to whoever was unlucky enough to be sitting next to her.
